title: Olympic Refuge Foundation Lived Experience Fellowship 2026–2027: Remote International Programme with Up to US$730 Monthly Stipend
summary: Applications are open for the Olympic Refuge Foundation Lived Experience Fellowship Programme 2026–2027, a part-time, remote opportunity for adults who have personally experienced displacement. This programme is intended to ensure that refugees, asylum seekers, stateless people, internally displaced persons and others affected by forced migration are directly involved in shaping research, policy, advocacy and practical solutions related to sport and displacement. The selected fellow will work with the Olympic Refuge Foundation Think Tank as a knowledge partner. Rather than being consulted only as a source of personal testimony, the fellow will help influence the framing, interpretation, production and communication of the Think Tank’s work. The programme will run from September 2026 to August 2027. Fellows will work remotely from their country of residence for approximately 10 to 20 hours per week. A monthly stipend ranging from US$150 to US$730 will be provided. According to the official Terms of Reference , applications must be submitted by midnight Eastern Time on 19 August 2026. Key Fellowship Information Programme: Olympic Refuge Foundation Lived Experience Fellowship Programme Organiser: Olympic Refuge Foundation Think Tank Programme administrator: Care and Protection of Children Learning Network Host institution of administrator: Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health Fellowship period: September 2026 to August 2027 Official start date: 15 September 2026 Working arrangement: Fully remote Time commitment: Approximately 10 to 20 hours per week Work location: Fellow’s country of residence Travel requirement: No travel is anticipated Financial support: US$150 to US$730 per month Minimum age: 18 years Academic degree required: No Application deadline: 19 August 2026 at midnight Eastern Time Virtual interviews: 24–28 August 2026 Notification of successful applicants: By 4 September 2026 The Terms of Reference do not specify the exact number of fellows who will be selected. About the Olympic Refuge Foundation The Olympic Refuge Foundation, commonly known as ORF, is an independent international nonprofit organisation based in Lausanne, Switzerland. It was founded by the International Olympic Committee in 2017 and is registered as a Swiss foundation. The Foundation works towards creating a society in which everyone can experience belonging through sport. Its mission focuses on developing a movement that helps young people affected by displacement to thrive through sport and physical activity. The Foundation conducts its work through three principal pillars: Catalyse, Sustain and Transform. Catalyse The Catalyse pillar serves as the Foundation’s innovation function. Through this pillar, ORF develops and tests new ideas addressing gaps between sport, humanitarian response and the needs of displaced communities. This work may involve collaboration with: Refugee-led organisations Nongovernmental organisations Humanitarian actors Community groups Research institutions Other strategic partners Evidence and data are used to evaluate these ideas, identify what works and determine whether successful approaches can be improved, adapted or expanded. Sustain The Sustain pillar concentrates on programmes and approaches that have already demonstrated positive results. It seeks to: Strengthen successful programmes Improve systems and operating processes Maintain programme quality Increase efficiency Incorporate effective practices Support the long-term continuation of proven initiatives Make successful programmes easier to expand This pillar helps ensure that effective programmes do not end after an initial pilot or funding period. Transform The Transform pillar focuses on broader policy and systems change. Through evidence, advocacy and partnerships, the Foundation works to influence public policies, institutional practices and humanitarian systems so that sport is recognised as an important component of crisis response. This work may include partnerships with UNHCR, cities and other organisations to integrate sport into areas such as: Mental health and psychosocial well-being Protection Social inclusion Urban inclusion Youth development Humanitarian response Recovery from displacement About the Olympic Refuge Foundation Think Tank Established in 2020, the Olympic Refuge Foundation Think Tank is a central part of the Foundation’s advocacy and knowledge-development work. It brings together expertise from: Academic institutions Nongovernmental organisations The public sector The private sector Young people with lived experience of displacement Researchers Advocates Practitioners The Think Tank strengthens the Olympic Refuge Foundation’s work in areas including programme design, evidence generation, research, advocacy and interdisciplinary practice. Its broader purpose is to improve understanding of how sport can support people affected by displacement and crisis. The Lived Experience Fellowship will help incorporate the knowledge of displaced people throughout the Think Tank’s work, including when: Identifying priority issues Designing research Interpreting findings Developing recommendations Creating policy outputs Communicating evidence Conducting advocacy Sharing findings with external audiences Role of the CPC Learning Network The Lived Experience Fellowship Programme will be administered by the Care and Protection of Children Learning Network on behalf of the Olympic Refuge Foundation. The CPC Learning Network is housed within Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health’s Program on Forced Migration and Health in New York, United States. The network was established in 2005 in response to the need for stronger measurement and evidence in child protection during emergencies. Its work connects knowledge and practice concerning: Children’s protection Children’s rights Development Well-being Humanitarian emergencies Crisis-affected communities The network’s work is guided by social justice, innovation, integrity and transformative relationships. CPC will support the fellowship’s administration, management, supervision and mentorship. A CPC staff member will also serve as the fellow’s principal contact for administrative matters. Why the Fellowship Was Created People with direct experience of displacement are often consulted during research or programme development. However, consultation does not always provide them with meaningful authority over decisions, priorities or final outputs. This fellowship seeks to address that problem by treating lived and living experience as a recognised form of expertise. The programme will give selected fellows a structured opportunity to lead, influence or jointly produce knowledge relating to: Sport Physical activity and movement Displacement Mental health Protection Social inclusion Recovery Policy Advocacy Systems change Fellows will work in an equitable partnership with Olympic Refuge Foundation staff, Think Tank members, mentors and relevant external partners. The programme is not designed simply to collect personal stories from displaced people. Instead, their knowledge will help determine how issues are examined, understood and addressed. Main Objectives of the Fellowship The Lived Experience Fellowship Programme aims to: Enable people with lived or living experience of displacement to influence the Think Tank’s objectives, analysis and outputs. Support knowledge development that is led or jointly produced by people with lived experience. Use this knowledge to inform the Olympic Refuge Foundation’s advocacy, strategy, programme learning and wider sector influence. Create opportunities for fellows to produce or contribute to research, policy, advocacy, storytelling or creative outputs. Allow fellows to join an existing Think Tank project or contribute to an established policy or advocacy priority. Support the development of a focused fellowship project where this is practical. Improve the relevance, quality and legitimacy of Think Tank outputs by incorporating lived-experience expertise throughout the process. Provide fellows with mentorship, peer learning and professional-development opportunities. Connect fellows with practitioners, researchers, organisations and advocates from different sectors. Help the Foundation evaluate how lived experience can more effectively influence its systems, strategies and decision-making. Scope of the Fellow’s Work The fellow’s specific area of work will be decided collaboratively at the beginning of the programme. The decision-making process will involve: The fellow Olympic Refuge Foundation staff Assigned mentors CPC administrators A relevant Think Tank working group, where applicable The selected focus should reflect the fellow’s interests, skills, experience and preferred area of contribution while remaining aligned with Think Tank priorities. Fellows will participate as knowledge partners capable of influencing how the Think Tank frames, interprets and communicates its work. Depending on the agreed work plan, the fellow may: Lead or jointly lead a small research project. Develop or contribute to a policy initiative. Participate in advocacy activities. Produce a storytelling or creative project. Contribute expertise to one or more Think Tank priorities. Develop outputs with Foundation staff, Think Tank members or external partners. Participate in Think Tank meetings. Join selected working-group discussions. Take part in informal learning activities. Help interpret or validate research findings. Review whether findings accurately reflect displaced communities’ experiences. Contribute to blogs, presentations or webinars. Participate in policy dialogues. Help produce multimedia content. Support the development of advocacy materials. Expected Fellowship Deliverables The final deliverables will be agreed during the first month of the fellowship. They must be proportionate to: The part-time nature of the programme The fellow’s experience The fellow’s agreed area of work Available support The 12-month fellowship period The fellow’s personal circumstances Each fellow will be expected to complete at least two principal contributions. 1. One Substantive Fellowship Output The main output may be: A policy brief A research report A reflective essay A thought-leadership article A creative project A narrative output A multimedia product A practical resource A contribution to a larger Think Tank publication 2. One Dissemination or Engagement Contribution This may include: A presentation to the Think Tank A website or blog article Participation in a webinar A learning session Input into an advocacy initiative An internal reflection for the Olympic Refuge Foundation Contribution to a policy discussion Additional outputs may be developed if they are realistic and mutually agreed. However, additional work should not automatically become a condition for successfully completing the programme. Fellows should retain meaningful control over the format, framing and emphasis of their work. Fellowship Duration, Hours and Location The fellowship will run from September 2026 to August 2027. The official start date is 15 September 2026. Fellows will work part-time for approximately 10 to 20 hours per week. Because the programme is remote, work will be completed from the fellow’s country of residence. No travel is currently anticipated. Applicants should nevertheless be prepared to participate in: Online meetings Virtual interviews Remote mentorship Collaborative online work Think Tank discussions Activities involving different time zones Work Plan and Reporting Arrangements During the first month, the fellow will develop a flexible work plan with CPC administrators, Olympic Refuge Foundation staff and assigned mentors. The work plan will establish: The fellow’s focus area Proposed outputs Support requirements Meeting schedule Relevant Think Tank priorities Research or project-planning requirements A realistic timetable The plan should balance the fellow’s interests and lived-experience expertise with what can realistically be completed and what would be useful to the Think Tank. The fellow and mentors will provide regular progress updates covering matters such as: Research activities Written outputs Thought-leadership work Event contributions Challenges Support requirements Upcoming deliverables Mentorship and Professional Support Each fellow will receive support from two dedicated mentors: One mentor from the Olympic Refuge Foundation Think Tank One mentor from the CPC Learning Network Following selection, fellows will be invited to identify preferred mentors or relevant areas of expertise. The programme will then seek to match fellows with appropriate mentors. Mentorship will be treated as a two-way learning process. Mentors will offer: Guidance Feedback Technical support Professional advice Assistance with research priorities Help with project planning Support in developing outputs At the same time, fellows will contribute lived-experience knowledge capable of strengthening the mentors’ understanding, assumptions and professional practices. Fellows will generally meet: Their supervisors once or twice each month Their mentors at least once every month These meetings will be used to review progress, discuss difficulties, receive feedback and adjust the work plan where necessary. Fellowship Supervision The fellow will be supervised jointly by designated members of: The Olympic Refuge Foundation Think Tank The CPC Learning Network Other relevant Olympic Refuge Foundation teams A designated CPC staff member will be the primary administrative and management contact. Supervisors will provide guidance concerning: Research priorities Project planning Deliverables Scheduling Reporting Participation in Think Tank activities Who Is Eligible to Apply? The opportunity is exclusively available to people with lived or living experience of displacement. This includes individuals who have personally experienced: Forced migration Refugeehood Asylum seeking Statelessness Internal displacement Crisis-affected mobility Other closely related forms of displacement Applicants must be at least 18 years old when they submit their application. Someone who professionally supports displaced people but has not personally experienced displacement does not satisfy the programme’s central eligibility requirement. Required Interests, Skills and Potential Applicants must demonstrate a strong interest in how sport, physical activity or movement can support people affected by crisis or displacement. They should also demonstrate: An ability to reflect critically on lived experience. An ability to connect personal experience with wider policy, advocacy, practice or systems-change issues. Sufficient English to complete administrative processes and participate in fellowship activities. Experience or potential in at least one relevant field. An interest in collaborating respectfully with people from different backgrounds and disciplines. Willingness to participate in online meetings. Willingness to participate in mentorship and co-production processes. Relevant fields may include: Research Writing Storytelling Advocacy Community leadership Programme implementation Youth engagement Creative practice Communications Policy Volunteering Informal community work Applicants do not necessarily need extensive professional experience. Demonstrated potential in one or more of these areas may be considered. Are Academic Qualifications Required? Formal academic qualifications are not required. Applicants do not need: A bachelor’s degree A master’s degree A postgraduate qualification Formal research training Academic publications Published research outputs The Olympic Refuge Foundation recognises that displacement may interrupt education, employment and professional development. Relevant expertise may therefore have been developed through: Community leadership Advocacy Creative practice Informal learning Professional employment Volunteer work Research Personal lived experience Applicants will not be disadvantaged because they do not have polished written or spoken English. Support with writing, editing or publication may be provided where necessary. Monthly Stipend The fellow will receive a monthly stipend ranging from US$150 to US$730. The exact amount will be determined according to the World Bank income classification of the fellow’s current country of residence. The stipend is therefore based on where the fellow currently lives, rather than necessarily being based on citizenship or country of origin. The Terms of Reference do not specify: The exact stipend for each income category Tax treatment Bank-transfer costs Country-specific reporting requirements Whether additional equipment or internet support will be provided Applicants should seek clarification if any of these matters would affect their ability to participate. Application Requirements Applicants must prepare the following materials. 1. Resume, CV or Experience Summary Applicants must submit a short resume, CV or summary of relevant experience consisting of no more than two pages. It may include: Formal employment Informal experience Community work Advocacy Creative work Volunteer experience Professional experience Lived-experience expertise 2. Statement of Interest Applicants must submit a short statement explaining: Why they are interested in the programme. How their lived or living experience informs their interest in the Think Tank. What perspective, knowledge or experience they could contribute. The statement must be in English and may be submitted as either: A written response of up to 500 words; or An audio or video response of up to three minutes. 3. Relevant Work Sample Where available, applicants should submit one example of relevant work. The sample may be in: English French Spanish Possible work samples include: Writing Research Advocacy materials Creative work Community-leadership materials Presentations Programme documents Multimedia content Other relevant outputs A written sample must not exceed three pages. An excerpt from a longer document may be used. An audio, video or multimedia submission must be limited to three minutes. If the original material is longer, the applicant should identify the specific three-minute section that reviewers should assess. 4. Two Referees Applicants must provide contact information for two referees. Referees may come from: Professional settings Academic institutions Community organisations Volunteer activities Advocacy groups Other relevant organisations Referees must not be directly related to the applicant. Artificial Intelligence Disclosure Requirement Applicants must disclose if they have used artificial intelligence for language or grammar assistance. AI-supported grammar or language correction is permitted and will not reduce an applicant’s score when properly disclosed. However, excessively generic responses or applications that appear to have been generated entirely by AI will not be considered. Applicants should ensure that their submission reflects: Their own experiences Their natural communication style Specific examples from their life or work Their genuine reasons for applying Their understanding of the programme The assessors explicitly value an applicant’s own words, even when those words contain minor errors, more than a polished but impersonal AI-generated application. Reasonable Accommodations Reasonable accommodations are available for qualified applicants with disabilities. Applicants requiring assistance to participate fully in the selection process should contact: connect@cpcln.org Candidates are advised to request any necessary accommodation before the application deadline. Application and Selection Process Applications must be submitted through the official online portal. After submission, CPC staff will conduct an administrative review to determine whether: The applicant has responded to the call. All required materials have been submitted. The application is complete. The central eligibility conditions have been met. Applications passing the administrative review will be assessed and scored by two reviewers. Shortlisted candidates will be invited to a virtual interview during the week beginning 24 August 2026. Final selection will consider: The applicant’s eligibility and qualifications Relevant skills and experience Demonstrated potential Statement of interest Written, audio or video sample Interview performance Alignment with Olympic Refuge Foundation priorities Successful applicants will be notified by 4 September 2026. If the programme receives a particularly strong group of applications, suitable candidates who are not selected may be invited to be considered for future opportunities. This would remain subject to: Funding availability Strategic alignment The applicant’s consent Important Dates Application deadline: 19 August 2026 at midnight Eastern Time, New York Virtual interviews: 24–28 August 2026 Successful applicants notified: By 4 September 2026 Fellowship start date: 15 September 2026 Fellowship end date: August 2027 Applicants in other time zones should carefully convert the deadline and submit early to avoid missing it because of a time-zone misunderstanding or technical problem. Principles Guiding the Programme The fellowship will operate according to several important principles: Equity Respect Reciprocity Safeguarding Trauma-informed practice Meaningful participation Personal agency Collaborative learning Fellows must be able to participate in ways that are safe, meaningful and realistic. The Olympic Refuge Foundation, CPC Learning Network and Think Tank members will be responsible for ensuring that fellows are not expected to: Represent every refugee or displaced person Speak on behalf of all displaced communities Disclose personal experiences they do not wish to share Relive traumatic experiences solely for institutional purposes The fellow’s lived experience will be respected as professional and practical knowledge that can improve decisions and outputs. How to Apply Eligible applicants should complete the official online application form . Before submitting, applicants should: Confirm that they have personal lived or living experience of displacement. Read the complete Terms of Reference. Prepare a resume or experience summary of no more than two pages. Prepare a personal statement of up to 500 words or three minutes. Select a relevant work sample, where available. Identify two appropriate referees who are not directly related to them. Disclose any use of AI for language or grammar support. Review the application for completeness. Submit before midnight Eastern Time on 19 August 2026. Questions about the programme may be sent to connect@cpcln.org . Why This Opportunity Matters The Olympic Refuge Foundation Lived Experience Fellowship creates a formal route through which displaced people can influence research, policy, advocacy and programme design. Its significance lies in recognising that institutions cannot develop fully effective responses to displacement without involving people who have experienced those systems and challenges personally. The fellowship combines: Lived experience Sport and physical activity Research Policy development Advocacy Creative communication Community leadership Professional mentorship This approach can help produce policies and programmes that are more realistic, relevant and responsive to the needs of displaced communities. Conclusion The Olympic Refuge Foundation Lived Experience Fellowship Programme 2026–2027 is an important international opportunity for adults who have personally experienced displacement and want to use their knowledge to shape research, advocacy, policy and practice through sport. The programme does not require formal academic qualifications, published research or postgraduate education. Instead, it values knowledge developed through lived experience, community leadership, advocacy, volunteering, creative practice, informal learning and professional work. Selected fellows will receive two mentors, professional-development support, access to the Olympic Refuge Foundation Think Tank and a monthly stipend of US$150 to US$730. They will work remotely for approximately 10 to 20 hours per week from September 2026 to August 2027. Eligible candidates should prepare an authentic and experience-based application and submit it by midnight Eastern Time on 19 August 2026. For more global opportunities, click HERE . title: Introduction to Sports for Climate Action Online Course 2026: Enroll in the Free UN Climate Change & UNITAR Sustainability Training with Optional Digital Certification
summary: Climate change is reshaping every sector of society, and the world of sports is no exception. From extreme weather disrupting major sporting events to the environmental impact of stadiums, travel, and sporting infrastructure, the sports industry faces significant climate-related challenges. Recognizing both the responsibility and the opportunity that sports have in driving positive environmental change, the United Nations Climate Change (UNFCCC) has launched the Introduction to Sports for Climate Action online course. Developed under the Sports for Climate Action Initiative , this self-paced online learning program equips sports professionals, organizations, students, policymakers, and climate enthusiasts with practical knowledge about sustainability in sports. The course forms the first part of a two-course learning series and introduces learners to the relationship between sports and climate change while offering practical solutions that can help transform the sector into a more sustainable and climate-resilient industry. Whether you work in sports management, coach athletes, organize sporting events, study environmental science, or simply have a passion for sustainability, this course provides an excellent opportunity to strengthen your understanding of climate action in sports while earning a United Nations digital certificate. About the Introduction to Sports for Climate Action Course The Introduction to Sports for Climate Action is a self-paced online course developed by the UN Climate Change Sports for Climate Action Initiative in technical collaboration with the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) and with financial support from adidas . The course is designed to increase climate literacy within the sports community and inspire meaningful action toward reducing greenhouse gas emissions while strengthening resilience against climate impacts. Sports influence millions of people globally. Beyond entertainment, sports have enormous potential to educate communities, inspire behavioural change, and promote sustainable development. However, the sports sector itself contributes significantly to greenhouse gas emissions through transportation, venue operations, construction, energy consumption, waste generation, and event logistics. At the same time, climate change threatens sporting activities through: Rising temperatures Heatwaves affecting athletes and spectators Flooding of sports facilities Wildfires Poor air quality Water shortages Severe storms disrupting competitions Environmental degradation affecting outdoor sports This course explores both sides of this relationship and demonstrates how sports organizations can become leaders in climate action. Background of the Sports for Climate Action Initiative The Sports for Climate Action Framework was launched by UN Climate Change in 2018 . Its primary objective is to unite sports organizations, governing bodies, teams, clubs, event organizers, sponsors, and stakeholders around shared climate commitments that contribute to the goals of the Paris Agreement. The initiative encourages sports organizations to: Reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Promote environmental sustainability. Build climate resilience. Raise public awareness about climate change. Inspire climate action among fans and communities. The Introduction to Sports for Climate Action course serves as one of the educational tools supporting this global initiative. Why This Course Matters Climate change is one of the defining global challenges of the 21st century. Sports organizations have unique platforms capable of influencing billions of people worldwide. This course helps learners understand: Why sports organizations should become climate leaders. How climate change is already affecting sporting events. The environmental footprint of sports activities. Ways sports can support climate adaptation and mitigation. Individual actions everyone can take to make sports more sustainable. The knowledge gained can support organizations seeking to improve sustainability strategies while helping individuals become advocates for greener sporting practices. Course Objectives Upon completing the course, learners will be able to: Understand how sports both contribute to and are affected by climate change. Explain what is at stake for communities as climate impacts intensify. Describe how climate change affects different populations and vulnerable groups. Discuss practical climate strategies within the sports industry. Recognize opportunities for sports organizations to reduce emissions. Identify actions that make sporting activities greener and more resilient. Encourage sustainable behaviour among athletes, supporters, and sporting communities. Course Structure The learning programme is designed to be completed in approximately 1 hour and 30 minutes . It includes four comprehensive learning modules followed by a final assessment. Module 1: Game Changer – The Role of Sports in Climate Action This introductory module explores: The connection between sports and climate change The responsibility of sports organizations Climate leadership within the sports sector Global climate commitments Why sports are important drivers of social transformation Module 2: Greening the Game – Reducing Sports Carbon Footprint This module examines practical methods for reducing emissions generated by sports. Topics include: Carbon emissions in sporting events Sustainable event planning Energy efficiency Transportation solutions Waste management Sustainable infrastructure Resource efficiency Module 3: The Climate Playbook – Building Sports Resilience Climate adaptation is increasingly important for sports organizations. Learners explore: Climate risk assessment Preparing for extreme weather Building resilient sports facilities Protecting athletes and spectators Long-term sustainability planning Module 4: Playing for the Planet – The Power of Sports The final learning module highlights the broader influence of sports. Topics include: Public engagement Behavioural change Climate advocacy Community leadership Environmental awareness campaigns Partnerships for sustainability Final Quiz After completing all modules, participants take a final assessment. To successfully complete the course: Achieve a minimum score of 70% . Learners receive three attempts to pass the assessment. Interactive Learning Experience The course offers an engaging online learning environment that includes: Interactive videos Knowledge checks Practical exercises Case studies Additional learning resources Self-paced progression Participants can complete the course whenever it suits their schedule. Digital Certificate After successfully passing the final quiz, participants become eligible to receive the official UNITAR Digital Certificate of Completion . Important certification information includes: Minimum passing score: 70% Maximum quiz attempts: 3 Certificate fee: USD 30 Certificate available after successful payment Certificate can be downloaded digitally Digital certification allows participants to verify and share their achievement professionally. Course Languages The course is currently available in: English Spanish This allows learners from different regions to participate more easily. Course Duration The estimated completion time is: Approximately 1 hour and 30 minutes Because the programme is self-paced, learners can complete it according to their own schedule. Who Should Take This Course? The course is ideal for a broad audience interested in sustainability and sports, including: Sports administrators Sports federation staff Event organizers Coaches Athletes Environmental professionals Climate advocates Sustainability officers University students Researchers Policymakers NGOs Government officials Sports clubs Volunteers Anyone interested in climate action and sustainable sports. Benefits of Taking the Course Participants will gain numerous benefits, including: Increased understanding of climate change. Knowledge of sustainable sports practices. Practical tools for reducing environmental impacts. Understanding of climate resilience strategies. Exposure to United Nations sustainability initiatives. Flexible online learning. Interactive educational resources. Optional internationally recognized UNITAR digital certification. Professional development opportunities. Improved sustainability leadership skills. Partners Behind the Course The programme was developed through collaboration among leading international organizations. Partners include: UN Climate Change (UNFCCC) United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) adidas (Financial Support) This collaboration combines expertise in climate science, education, sustainability, and sports. Why Sports Are Critical to Climate Action Sports have unparalleled global influence. Millions of people attend sporting events every year, while billions watch competitions through television and digital media. Athletes often serve as role models capable of inspiring environmental responsibility among fans and communities. By integrating sustainability into sporting activities, organizations can: Reduce carbon emissions. Promote sustainable lifestyles. Inspire behavioural change. Support climate education. Encourage responsible resource use. Build climate-resilient communities. This course empowers learners to become part of that global movement. How to Enroll Interested learners can: Visit the official course webpage. Create or log into their learning account. Enroll in the course. Complete all four modules. Pass the final quiz. Purchase the optional digital certificate after passing. ENROLL HERE Deadline There is no application or enrollment deadline . As a self-paced online course, learners can enroll at any time. Visit HERE to learn more about the Introduction to Sports for Climate Action Online Course 2026. Conclusion The Introduction to Sports for Climate Action provides an excellent opportunity for individuals and organizations to better understand the relationship between sports and climate change while learning practical strategies for building a more sustainable future. Developed by UN Climate Change in partnership with UNITAR and supported by adidas, the course combines expert knowledge with interactive learning to empower participants to become champions of environmental sustainability within the sports sector. Whether you are a sports professional, policymaker, student, researcher, or climate advocate, this course offers valuable insights into reducing emissions, strengthening resilience, and leveraging the power of sports to inspire climate action. With flexible self-paced learning, multilingual access, and an optional UN digital certificate, it is an ideal opportunity to build knowledge and contribute meaningfully to a low-carbon and climate-resilient future. title: Call for Applications: U.S. Democracy Reporting Grants 2026 – Pulitzer Center Funds Investigative Journalism on Democracy Issues
summary: The Pulitzer Center has officially opened applications for its U.S. Democracy Reporting Grants 2026 , providing funding opportunities for journalists, editors, and freelancers who are committed to producing impactful reporting on democracy-related issues in the United States. At a time when democratic institutions, elections, transparency, civil liberties, and government accountability remain central to public discourse, the Pulitzer Center is seeking ambitious journalism projects that investigate these critical issues. Rather than funding routine news coverage, the organization is looking for deeply researched, high-impact stories or series that can help audiences better understand how democracy functions and the challenges it faces. This funding opportunity offers journalists the financial support necessary to pursue extensive investigations, produce multimedia reporting, conduct data-driven research, and engage communities through meaningful journalism projects. About the Pulitzer Center U.S. Democracy Reporting Grants The Pulitzer Center s Democracy Reporting Grants are designed to support in-depth journalism that examines the state of democracy in the United States. The grants encourage reporters to investigate complex issues that affect democratic systems and institutions while producing stories that inform the public and promote accountability. Successful applicants will receive funding to pursue reporting projects that require significant research, travel, data analysis, multimedia production, or audience engagement initiatives. Rather than supporting ongoing newsroom beats or everyday reporting assignments, the Pulitzer Center seeks projects that provide fresh perspectives, uncover overlooked issues, and contribute meaningful reporting on democracy. Purpose of the Democracy Reporting Grants The program aims to strengthen public understanding of democracy by supporting journalism that: Investigates democratic institutions. Explores voting rights and election transparency. Examines government accountability. Reports on civil liberties and free speech. Holds public institutions accountable. Explains complex governance issues. Produces impactful investigative journalism. Engages communities through trustworthy reporting. The initiative recognizes that high-quality journalism plays a critical role in strengthening democratic societies by providing citizens with accurate, well-researched, and independent reporting. Reporting Themes the Pulitzer Center Wants to Support Applicants are encouraged to submit ambitious proposals covering one or more of the following areas. 1. Voting Rights Projects may investigate: Voter access Election laws Voter suppression Electoral participation Changes in voting systems Election administration 2. Civil Rights and Free Speech The Pulitzer Center welcomes stories examining: Freedom of expression Civil liberties Constitutional rights Public demonstrations Media freedom Government restrictions 3. Election Transparency Possible reporting topics include: Election integrity Transparency in election processes Public confidence in elections Election oversight Election management systems 4. Government Accountability Journalists are encouraged to investigate how: Federal agencies carry out their responsibilities. State government agencies implement policies. Public institutions serve communities. Government decisions affect citizens. Accountability mechanisms function. What Kind of Projects Are Eligible? The Pulitzer Center is looking for ambitious reporting projects rather than routine journalism. Suitable projects include: Investigative reporting Long-form journalism Multimedia storytelling Documentary reporting Broadcast journalism Data journalism Cross-platform reporting Series of investigative stories Projects should provide substantial public value and offer meaningful insights into democracy-related issues. What the Grants Can Cover Grant funding may be used to support various reporting expenses, including: Travel Costs Applicants may request funding for travel required to complete reporting assignments. Research Expenses Funding can support: Specialized research Public records requests Archive access Document retrieval Data Analysis Applicants may receive support for: Record searches Data acquisition Data analysis Investigative research tools Visual Journalism Funding may also cover: Photography Videography Graphic production Multimedia storytelling Additional reporting assistance Audience Engagement The Pulitzer Center encourages initiatives that help journalists build stronger relationships with communities. Examples include: Public events Community discussions Audience engagement campaigns Educational activities Public presentations Expanding the Reach of Journalism The Pulitzer Center places significant importance on ensuring funded reporting reaches wide audiences. Applicants are encouraged to think beyond publication and consider strategies that increase the visibility and impact of their work. These strategies may include: Partnering with multiple news organizations. Publishing across digital platforms. Broadcast partnerships. Multimedia distribution. Social media campaigns. Community-focused outreach. Projects demonstrating a strong dissemination strategy may strengthen an application. Who Can Apply? The Pulitzer Center welcomes applications from: Staff reporters working in newsrooms. Editors working with reporting teams. Freelance journalists. Freelancers collaborating with established news organizations. Freelancers must work closely with a newsroom that has committed to editing and publishing the proposed reporting project. Projects may be published in: Print publications Online news platforms Multimedia platforms Television Radio Broadcast media Who Is Not Eligible? According to the call for applications, the Pulitzer Center is not seeking proposals for: Routine news coverage. Regular beat reporting. Permanent newsroom positions. Work submitted by individuals who are not journalists. Instead, applicants should focus on proposing significant investigative or explanatory reporting projects with broad public importance. Why This Opportunity Matters Producing high-quality investigative journalism often requires resources that many newsrooms and freelance journalists may not have. Through these grants, the Pulitzer Center helps journalists: Pursue ambitious investigations. Access specialized research resources. Conduct extensive reporting. Produce multimedia stories. Increase audience engagement. Build partnerships with other media organizations. Improve the impact and reach of important journalism. This support enables journalists to tell stories that might otherwise never be reported due to financial or logistical constraints. Application Deadline Deadline: August 31, 2026 The Pulitzer Center has indicated that applications will be reviewed on a rolling basis as they are received. Applicants are therefore encouraged to submit their proposals as early as possible rather than waiting until the deadline. How to Apply Interested applicants should prepare a compelling reporting proposal outlining: The story idea. Its significance. Reporting methodology. Expected impact. Budget requirements. Publication commitment from a newsroom (particularly for freelancers). Applicants can review the Pulitzer Center s application guidance and complete the official application through the organization s online application platform. APPLY HERE Additional Support Applicants with questions about the program may contact the Pulitzer Center s Senior Editor, Susan Ferriss, for clarification regarding the funding opportunity. However, the organization does not review draft applications before submission. Visit HERE to learn more about the U.S. Democracy Reporting Grants 2026. Conclusion The Pulitzer Center s U.S. Democracy Reporting Grants present an outstanding opportunity for journalists dedicated to producing impactful investigative reporting on democracy in the United States. By supporting ambitious reporting projects covering elections, civil rights, government accountability, transparency, and democratic institutions, the program helps strengthen public understanding of issues that shape society. Whether you are a newsroom reporter, editor, or freelance journalist collaborating with a publishing partner, this grant can provide the financial resources necessary to pursue meaningful investigations with lasting public impact. Since applications are reviewed as they arrive, prospective applicants are encouraged to begin preparing their proposals and submit them well before the August 31, 2026 deadline. title: Norec Grant for Work Exchange Cooperation 2026–2027: Apply for Up to 150,000 NOK to Develop International Work Exchange Partnerships for Sustainable Development
summary: The Norec Grant for Work Exchange Cooperation is now accepting applications for its Phase 1: Concept Development funding opportunity, offering organizations the chance to build strong international partnerships and develop innovative work exchange projects focused on sustainable development. The initiative supports organizations that are committed to creating meaningful global collaborations while providing young professionals with valuable international work experience. This grant serves as the first stage of a two-phase funding process and is specifically designed for new partnerships that intend to establish long-term international work exchange programmes beginning in August or September 2027 . Successful applicants in Phase 1 will receive financial support to jointly develop their project ideas before applying for full project implementation funding in Phase 2. Organizations from eligible countries that are passionate about sustainable development, youth empowerment, climate action, gender equality, and international cooperation are encouraged to submit their applications before the deadline. Application Deadline: 1 September 2026 (23:59 Central European Time CET). What is the Norec Grant for Work Exchange Cooperation? The Norec Grant for Work Exchange Cooperation is an international funding programme established to strengthen global partnerships through reciprocal work exchanges. Rather than simply funding development projects, Norec focuses on building institutional capacity by enabling organizations from different countries to exchange young professionals and volunteers who can share knowledge, skills, and experience. The programme supports Norway s broader international development policy while contributing to the achievement of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) . Its long-term objective is to strengthen organizations through mutual learning while creating opportunities for young people to gain practical international work experience that contributes to sustainable development. Unlike traditional aid programmes, the Norec model is based on reciprocity, ensuring that all participating organizations both contribute knowledge and benefit from the partnership. Purpose of the Grant The Norec grant has two primary objectives: Build strong and lasting global partnerships that promote institutional development. Create opportunities for young people to gain international work experience while contributing to sustainable development. These objectives contribute toward Norway s international development priorities, including: Economic development Poverty reduction Democracy Human rights Good governance Sustainable development Norec s Core Principles Norec s Core Principles is firmly grounded on Norec’s vision and theory of change and reflects two main principles: The programme is built around two important principles. 1. Reciprocity Every organization involved is considered an equal partner. Instead of one organization simply providing assistance to another, each partner contributes expertise, knowledge, and practical experience while simultaneously learning from the other organizations. This mutual exchange creates stronger institutions and more sustainable long-term partnerships. 2. Youth Participation Young people represent a significant proportion of the world s population but often have limited opportunities to participate in international decision-making and development initiatives. Through work exchanges lasting between six and twelve months, young professionals aged 18–35 gain valuable international experience while supporting sustainable development initiatives within host organizations. Thematic Priorities for 2026 Although applications addressing all Sustainable Development Goals are welcome, Norec has identified several priority themes for the 2026 funding cycle: Climate Climate adaptation Gender equality Sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) Projects addressing these areas may receive particular attention during assessment. Two-Phase Application Process The funding programme consists of two connected stages. Phase 1: Concept Development Applicants jointly submit a project concept describing their proposed work exchange partnership. If approved, organizations receive funding to: Meet in person Strengthen their partnership Develop the project concept Prepare a comprehensive Phase 2 application During this stage, Norec also provides guidance to help applicants design successful exchange projects. Phase 2: Project Implementation Organizations that successfully complete Phase 1 may submit a full implementation proposal. Approved partnerships receive funding to carry out their international work exchange programme. Who Can Apply? Applications must be submitted jointly by partnerships consisting of two or more legally registered organizations from different countries. Eligible organization types include: Civil society organizations Public institutions Private sector companies Multilateral organizations Global organizations Each organization must be legally registered under one of these categories. Organizational Capacity Requirements All partner organizations must demonstrate sufficient administrative and financial capacity. Requirements include: A Board of Directors or Trustees (where applicable) A physical office Suitable workspace for exchange participants Digital accounting software (Excel alone is not accepted) Ability to receive international funding Audited annual financial statements no older than 18 months At least three full-time salaried employees working across programme delivery, management, and administration (with limited exceptions) Geographic Eligibility Projects must be implemented in countries that qualify for Norwegian Official Development Assistance (ODA). Norec gives priority to countries where Norway already has established development cooperation ( Norec’s’ partner list ). During assessment, Norec also considers: Visa feasibility Security conditions Travel permissions Additional Eligibility Requirements Applicants must also satisfy several important conditions. Organizations: Must not be under investigation by Norec. Must not have outstanding reimbursement claims. Must comply with labour, health, safety and environmental legislation. Must maintain policies against sexual exploitation, abuse, harassment and corruption. Must follow responsible business practices where applicable. Read more on Norec’s minimum ethical principles . Project Requirements The proposed project must: Address a clearly identified development need. Align with Norec s objectives. Comply with OECD/DAC Official Development Assistance (ODA) criteria . Promote sustainable development. Demonstrate strong reciprocal partnerships. Commitment to Inclusion Norec actively encourages applications from: Organizations that have not traditionally participated in international development cooperation. Organizations representing marginalized or vulnerable groups. This reflects Norec s commitment to the principle of Leave No One Behind . How Applications Are Evaluated Eligible applications are assessed using several criteria. Administrative Capacity Organizations must demonstrate effective governance, financial systems, and project management capacity. Partnership Strength Applications should clearly explain: Each partner s role Mutual benefits Joint ownership Collaborative planning Learning Objectives Projects should include: Realistic goals Measurable indicators Clear target groups Organizational learning outcomes Innovation Projects should demonstrate: Knowledge exchange Innovative approaches Institutional learning Potential for long-term impact Strategic Alignment The project should complement each organization s existing strategy and demonstrate why Norec funding adds value. Sustainability Applicants should explain how project outcomes will continue after funding ends. Participant Support Organizations must provide detailed plans covering: Recruitment Mentoring Integration Learning activities Support before, during and after exchanges Risk Management Applications should identify and mitigate risks relating to: Human rights Gender equality Climate Environmental protection Corruption Financial management Cost Effectiveness Budgets should justify every proposed expenditure and demonstrate efficient use of funding. Alignment with Norec Priorities Projects that support Norec s thematic priorities and portfolio balance will receive stronger consideration. Assessment of Returning Applicants Organizations that previously received Norec funding will also be evaluated on: Performance under previous grants Financial management Administrative compliance Participant support Partnership communication Innovation Ability to build upon previous achievements Available Funding Successful Phase 1 applicants may receive: Up to 150,000 Norwegian Kroner (NOK) or the equivalent amount in USD. Funding can cover: Partner meetings International travel Accommodation Daily allowances Required visas Vaccinations All budgets must follow Norec s official templates and guidelines . Important Dates Activity Date Phase 1 application deadline 1 September 2026 Decision notification Within 3 months Phase 2 application deadline (invited applicants) 1 February 2027 Expected exchange start August/September 2027 How to Apply Applicants should complete their application through Norec s online application portal. Before applying, organizations should ensure they: Form an eligible international partnership. Develop a joint project concept. Prepare the required organizational documentation. Complete the official budget template. Submit the application before the deadline. Norec has indicated that applicants must use its new digital application portal for Phase 1 submissions. APPLY NOW Conclusion The Norec Grant for Work Exchange Cooperation presents a significant opportunity for organizations seeking to build impactful international partnerships while empowering young professionals through reciprocal work exchanges. With funding of up to 150,000 NOK available during the Concept Development phase, organizations can establish the foundations for long-term collaboration that advances sustainable development, institutional learning, and global knowledge exchange. Organizations with strong international ambitions, a commitment to youth participation, and innovative ideas aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals should begin preparing their applications well before the 1 September 2026 deadline. Successful Phase 1 applicants will not only receive financial support to refine their project ideas but also position themselves for larger implementation funding in Phase 2, paving the way for meaningful international cooperation beginning in 2027.
